god.title: Sharing Jesus with a skeptic
god.intro: The debate is almost never the real thing in the room. This is about being the Christian who is honest about what is hard, who does not use arguments they have not checked, and who is still there next year.
god.html:
Work out which one you are talking to
You, early on

"What made you land where you are? I would rather hear how you got there than argue about the arguments."

There is no generic atheist. There are at least three, and they need three different conversations. Get this wrong and everything else you say is aimed at nobody.

The first was in church and got hurt. A cover-up. A father who preached it and did not live it. A prayer that went unanswered at the worst possible moment. This person already knows the arguments and is not moved by them. Ask what happened, then be quiet for a long time.

The second reasoned their way out. Evidence, philosophy, science. They have usually read more on their own side than you have. They deserve real sources and real arguments, not a summary of a summary.

The third never thought about it at all. No wound and no argument. Religion has simply never been a live option. Debate bounces off, because there is nothing yet to debate. What moves this person is a real question, a real friendship, and a life that visibly costs something.

One rule covers all three. Never treat I do not believe as a bluff. It is not a pose, a rebellion, or a hidden belief being suppressed. Take it at face value. If you cannot, you are not in a conversation. You are running a script.

Work out which one you have before you decide what to bring. The wrong opening is not neutral. It tells the person you were not listening.

Most conversations also move between the three. A question about physics can be a grief wearing a coat, and a grief can harden into a syllogism over time.

So keep checking. The person you started talking to in March may not be the one in front of you in June.

The invitation to work toward
You, in time

"Would you read one Gospel with me? Luke, or Mark. Then just tell me what you actually think of him."

Most skeptics have opinions about Christianity and have never read a Gospel straight through as an adult.

The offer is unusual because it asks for their judgment rather than their agreement. It also puts the person in front of them instead of the argument.

Aim one notch, not the whole distance. Moving someone from obviously false to worth thinking about is a real win for one evening.

Say out loud that a single evening is not going to settle it. That removes the pressure which makes people defend positions they do not really hold.

Then keep your word. Ask again in a month, not in an hour.

Trying to close the whole gap at once produces someone who now has a reason to avoid the subject with you.

What actually reaches a skeptic
1

Conceding what is genuinely hard, first

Evil. Divine hiddenness. The conquest passages. The census of Quirinius. Name these before you are pushed. A person who admits a difficulty is worth hearing on everything else. A person with an instant answer for everything is worth hearing on nothing.

2

Arguing from sources that want another answer

Bart Ehrman on the crucifixion. Gerd Lüdemann on what the disciples experienced. The early dating of the creed in 1 Corinthians 15. The Tel Dan Stele. All of it comes from outside the church, and that is why it travels.

3

Asking what happened to them

Behind a large share of atheism is a story rather than an argument. The syllogism is real and deserves an answer. It is usually not the thing that needs answering first. Ask, and then wait longer than feels comfortable.

4

Being unembarrassing

The fastest way to lose this is a bad argument delivered with confidence. Retire the banana. Retire the thermodynamics claim. Retire the line about no transitional fossils. Retire the Darwin deathbed legend. Dropping them costs you nothing.

The method

Say you do not know, when you do not

Then go and find out, and come back with it. This is the most credibility-building thing available in these conversations. It is available to anyone, whatever they have read.

Know their best arguments better than they do

Read Graham Oppy rather than a Christian summary of Oppy. Watch Sean Carroll debate William Lane Craig. If you cannot state the argument accurately before answering it, you are not ready to answer it.

Take the hiddenness argument seriously

Schellenberg on divine hiddenness and the evidential problem of evil are the two strongest arguments in living atheist philosophy. Neither has a tidy answer. Say so, give the real response, and name its limits.

Never tell them what they secretly believe

You know God exists and are suppressing it. You just want to sin. Atheism takes more faith. Each line tells your friend you are talking to a stereotype instead of to them. Each one ends the conversation while sounding, to you, like a point scored.

Not the wager as an opener

Pascal never built it as an opener. It speaks to someone already persuaded that the odds are not trivial. Led with, it sounds like an invitation to fake a belief for insurance. That is bad philosophy and worse theology.

Not evolution as the battlefield

Christianity is not committed to a six-thousand-year-old earth, and large parts of the church never thought it was. Fight there and the actual claim never gets discussed. The claim is a man executed under Pilate and seen alive afterwards.

The sentence that buys the most credit
You, honestly

"That is the strongest argument against what I believe, and I do not think it has a tidy answer."

Say that when it is true, and it will often be true.

It buys more credibility than any rebuttal, and it costs nothing you should want. The Canaanite passages are hard. Unanswered prayer in a hospital is hard.

Then give the real response, with its limits named. On suffering, remember that the argument in front of you may be standing in for a funeral you have not heard about yet.

And when the ground is cleared, stop arguing. Nobody has ever been argued into the kingdom. The evidence only clears space for a person.

The census of Quirinius is a genuine historical problem. The honest answer lays out the options and admits that none of them is clean.

The conquest passages are worse, and no short reply does them justice. Do not reach for one.

What you are offering in the end is not a proposition. It is the man whose execution under Pilate even your friend already accepts as history.

Notice also what you are not asked to do. You are not asked to defend every Christian, every church, or every bad argument you have ever heard made.

Say that plainly when it comes up. A lot of what your friend rejected is worth rejecting, and agreeing with them costs you nothing.

The one claim you cannot give away is the empty tomb. Everything else can be held loosely while you work out together what is actually being argued.

And if the conversation dies, leave the door open rather than the last word. You are trying to be there in five years, not to finish tonight.

How it actually goes

"One of the most certain facts of history is that Jesus was crucified on orders of the Roman prefect."

— Bart Ehrman, agnostic, and the most-read skeptical New Testament scholar alive

The five questions that do the most work

  1. "What made you land where you are?" Ask it first, every time, and listen to the whole answer without preparing a reply. It tells you which of the three conversations you are actually in. Nothing you say before you know that is aimed at anything.
  2. "Do you think Jesus existed and was crucified?" Almost every informed skeptic says yes, and Ehrman says it in print. Start on shared ground and move one step at a time. That is the only version of this argument that has ever worked on anybody.
  3. "What would it take to change your mind?" It is a fair question because you have to answer it about yourself too. Paul already did, in 1 Corinthians 15:17. If neither of you can answer it, you are not arguing. You are in a standoff with better manners.
  4. "If it were true, would you want it to be?" This is the most revealing question here. The answer separates an intellectual obstacle from a grief or an injury. Those two need completely different things from you, and mixing them up wastes years.
  5. "Can I tell you the part I cannot explain away?" Then tell them why you are still in this, in your own words, briefly. Testimony is not proof and should not be offered as proof. It is evidence that a real person finds it worth staking a life on.

Start here

Read Arguments to retire before anything else. It is the highest-return page on the site. Then take the Easter path, which covers what skeptical historians grant about AD 30 and what explains it. Every case ends with a scripted back-and-forth, with the strongest naturalistic reply included.
